title: The Trompowsky Attack
description: This opening helped Levy reach 2200 elo. The goal is to prevent your opponents from playing many theoretical defenses, instead fighting on your terms.

r1b1k2r/pp2qppp/2n1p3/2ppP3/3Pn3/2PB1P2/.text:
Because our knight is on e2, which lends g3 some protection, we can now push f3. 

9...Ng5 gives us the win with 10.h4. 

And 9...Qh4+ can now be blocked with 10.g3.

r1b1k2r/pp2qppp/2n1p3/2ppP3/3Pn3/2PB4/PP.text: The knight is another attacker on d4, but it's sufficiently defended.

r1b1k2r/pppp1ppp/1nn1p3/4P3/1qPP4/8/PPQN.text:
Black attacks d4.

But we're able to develop and defend the pawn.

r1b2rk1/pppp1ppp/1nn1p3/4P3/1qPP4/3B1N2/.text:
Our huge space advantage on both sides of the board is no laughing matter. It's the reason the engine says we have an edge. 

We can go a3 and b4, but if 10...g6 we can also play 11.h4. Black's king can get into serious trouble!

r1bq1rk1/ppp1nppp/2n1p3/4P3/6Q1/2NB1N2/P.text:
The engine gives us a +2 position already. 

The powerful e5-pawn makes any defense of the king extremely difficult. 

We will castle kingside, play Ng5 and attack that h7-pawn until Black's defenses crumble.

r1bq1rk1/ppp1nppp/2n1p3/4P3/6Q1/2NB4/PPP.text: Black develops another piece and targets e5.

rnb1k2r/pp1pqppp/1n2p3/2p1P3/2PP4/3B4/PP.text:
7...c5 now is smart if we fall for it: Black wants to undermine our central pawn chain.

We won't take on c5. 

Rather, we'll counter with 8.Qg4 and attack g7.

rnb1k2r/pp2qppp/1n1pp3/8/2PP4/3B4/PP3PPP.text:
Black recaptures. 

If 8...Qxd6 there's 9.c5.

We'll continue developing, and our center is still big. 

Black has a lot of catching up to do. This is one of the benefits of this variation.

rnb1k2r/pp2qppp/4p3/2ppP3/3Pn3/2PB4/PP3P.text:
Black undermines our center. 

But our powerful pawn chain holds firm. 

We can even develop and support it further with the knight. 

With our development completed, it's almost time to go for f3 and h4.

rnb1k2r/ppp1qppp/1n1pp3/4P3/2PP4/3B4/PP3.text:
Black pushes trying to undermine our center. 

In this case, because Black hasn't committed to castling, we'll take on d6.

rnb1k2r/ppp1qppp/4p3/3pP3/3Pn3/2P5/PP3PP.text:
Black supports their knight. 

Their big problem is that it has no retreat squares if attacked by our pawns.

We'll develop the bishop and start putting some pressure on the knight. 

We cannot go f3 and h4 too early because Black has ...Qh4+ ideas and we must be careful!

rnb1k2r/pppp1ppp/1n2p3/4P3/1qPP4/8/PP1N1.text:
The knight moves to b6, but Black's pressure amounts to nothing.

With Qc2, we can simply overprotect the c4-pawn and start getting all of our forces mobilized.

rnb1k2r/pppp1ppp/4p3/3nP3/1qPP4/8/PP3PPP.text:
Black can attack the b2-pawn with check.

But as long as we develop and have a tempo on the d5-knight, we don't care about b2.

rnb1k2r/ppppqppp/1n2p3/4P3/2PP4/8/PP3PPP.text:
The knight on b6 is not so effective. It attacks the c4-pawn, but we are defending it.

We can simply develop our bishop to d3, aiming at h7 for when Black castles.

rnb1k2r/ppppqppp/4p3/3nP3/3P4/8/PPP2PPP/.text:
5...Qxe7 is the most popular way to recapture. 

After all, it makes sense to want to get another piece out of its home square.

We'll attack the knight and force it to a worse square.

rnb1k2r/ppppqppp/4p3/4P3/3Pn3/8/PPP2PPP/.text:
Black recaptures.

Since we traded the dark-squared bishop, we don't mind putting our pawns on dark squares. 

This is a common strategy you'll see in the Trompowsky. 

Tactically, we also prevent ...Qb4+.

rnb2rk1/pp1pqppB/1n2p3/4P3/2Pp2Q1/5N2/PP.text:
The Greek Gift! 

We are completely winning.

rnb2rk1/pp1pqppp/1n2p3/2p1P3/2PP2Q1/3B4/.text:
White castles. 

Recall that the ingredients for the Greek Gift are almost all on the board.

We'll complete the configuration by developing our knight to f3.

rnb2rk1/pp1pqppp/1n2p3/4P3/2Pp2Q1/3B1N2/.text: Taking on d4 for example loses.

rnb2rk1/pp2qppp/1n1pp3/8/2PP4/3B1N2/PP3P.text:
And so do we. 

We can now expect a promising middlegame thanks to the fact that we have taken the game in a direction that's favorable for us.

Re1, Nc3 or Nbd2, Qc2 and Rad1 are some simple yet effective plans.

rnbq1rk1/ppp1nppp/3pp3/4P3/3P2Q1/3B4/PPP.text:
Black castles.

We should just continue to develop.

rnbq1rk1/ppp1nppp/4p3/4p3/3P2Q1/2NB4/PPP.text:
This capture isn't a concern.

Our d-pawn can take the place of our e5-pawn.

rnbqk2r/ppp1nppp/3pp3/4P3/3P4/3B4/PPP2PP.text:
6...d6 is an attempt from Black to undermine our strong pawn chain. 

We of course will not capture on d6, because we would give up our pawn bridgehead on e5.

Instead, we'll develop our queen and attack g7.

rnbqk2r/ppppbppp/4p3/3nP1B1/3P4/8/PPP2PP.text:
This invites a trade of bishops. About 90% of games feature this move. 

The knight on d5 is centralized, but it can be kicked with moves like c4.

First, though, we have to trade.

rnbqk2r/ppppbppp/4p3/4P1B1/3Pn3/8/PPP2PP.text:
4...Ne4 is another square for the knight. Less than 10% of games go like this. 

The problem for Black is that nothing defends it.

First of all, we'll trade.

rnbqk2r/ppppbppp/4pn2/6B1/3PP3/8/PPP2PPP.text:
60% of games in the database feature 3...Be7.

Black unpins and now threatens e4.

We will take even more central space and defend our pawn in the process.

rnbqk2r/ppppnppp/4p3/4P3/3P4/8/PPP2PPP/R.text:
This is also possible and often played. 

Black figures that c4 is coming, so it's fine to move the knight backwards.

However, notice all the kingside space that our d4/e5 pawn duo gives us. 

After Bd3, our bishop points menacingly at the black kingside.

rnbqkb1r/pppp1ppp/4pn2/6B1/3P4/8/PPP1PPP.text:
Close to 3 million games in the online database go like this. This is 30% of the games recorded. 

Black wants to defend the knight so that the pawns aren't doubled.

3.e4 is now known as the Big Center Variation. 

Black cannot take on e4 because their knight is pinned.

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/5n2/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/R.text:
Black develops their knight.

This move is very flexible and can lead to various openings, e.g. King's Indian, Nimzo, Grunfeld, etc. 

The advantage of our Trompowsky is that we reduce Black's options.

2.Bg5 is the signature move. 

We may double the pawns, or simply have a pin on the knight after ...e6.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
The Trompowsky is an easy opening to learn with 1.d4. 

The main idea is that you'll play an early Bg5 against ...Nf6 with the idea of increasing your control of the center. 

In this study, we'll see the main line at the amateur level!

We'll begin with 1.d4.

r1b1k2r/pppp1pp1/2n1p2p/8/1b1PP3/2NQ4/PP.text:
This pawn cannot be taken without consequence.

After Nf3, the queen simply isn't getting back out.

r1b1k2r/pppp1pp1/2n1pq1p/8/1b1PP3/2NQ4/P.text:
This is the most popular move. 

Black develops and attacks d4.

We castle and defend our pawn.

r1b1k2r/pppp1pp1/2nbp2p/4P3/3P4/2NQ1N2/P.text:
But thanks to the fact we have a strong pawn duo, we can push e5 and attack the bishop. 

The queen is in a lot of trouble and we are winning.

r1b1k2r/pppp1pp1/2nbp2p/8/3PP3/2NQ1N2/PP.text: If we play Rd2 now, Bf4 pins our rook to the king.

r1b2rk1/pppp1pp1/2n1pq1p/8/1b1PP3/2NQ2P1.text:
We're going for f4, Nf3 and a kingside attack. 

Black's lack of space is evident here as well. We are better.

rn1qkb1r/pp1b1pp1/3pP2p/1Bp1P3/8/2N5/PPP.text:
We can play this in-between move and take on f7. 

Black is lost.

rn1qkb1r/pp1b1pp1/3pp2p/1BpPP3/8/2N5/PPP.text: If the bishop blocks, for instance, we don't have to trade right away because our knight on c3 defends our bishop.

rnb1k2r/ppp2pb1/3ppqpp/8/3PP3/2N5/PPPQ1P.text:
Black fianchettoes. 

However, the space advantage is becoming clear in this line also.

After f4, we have three strong central pawns.

rnb1k2r/pppp1pp1/4pq1p/8/1b1PP3/2N5/PPP2.text:
5...Bb4 is played almost 45% of the time. 

It's reasonable because Black doesn't want to be passive.

We'll defend our knight and prevent the doubled pawns.

6...0-0 and we can continue with our main plan of 0-0-0 and Nge2.

rnb1kb1r/pp1p1pp1/4pq1p/2p5/3PP3/2N5/PPP.text:
This move is very natural, and it's played around 10% of the time. 

The idea is to undermine our big center.

Since there were too many pieces converging on our d4-pawn, we'll attack one of them, the queen. 

It must now go to a worse square.

rnb1kb1r/ppp2p2/3ppqpp/8/3PP3/2N5/PPPQ1P.text:
The most common line now includes a fianchetto.

We castle.

rnb1kb1r/ppp2pp1/3ppq1p/8/3PP3/2N5/PPP2P.text:
5...d6 makes sense. 

At surface level, they are stopping the e5-push. But e5 is only one of our ideas. Another plan we have is Qd2, 0-0-0 and a kingside attack.

rnb1kb1r/pppp1pp1/4pq1p/8/3PP3/8/PPP2PPP.text:
The queen recaptures, but its pressure will never be the same as the knight's.

And we'll simply develop our knight so that both our central pawns are defended.

rnb2rk1/ppp2pb1/3ppqpp/8/3PPP2/2N2N2/PPP.text:
The engine gives us a big advantage here. 

Again, all because of our space advantage and our incoming attack on the kingside. We have g4 and h4-h5.

rnb2rk1/ppp2pb1/3ppqpp/8/3PPP2/2N5/PPPQ2.text: To stay alive, Black has to delay castling as long as possible, but the majority of intermediate players choose to castle to follow opening principles.

rnbqkb1r/pp1p1pp1/4p2p/2p1P3/3P4/2N5/PPP.text:
This is the reason why 5...c5 is bad. 

The queen can be kicked away, and we are left with two dynamic pawns as a result of our first 3 Trompowsky moves.

We can even push d5 and threaten d6 in some variations. 

This may cause Black to worry.

rnbqkb1r/pp3pp1/3pp2p/2pPP3/8/2N5/PPP2PP.text:
7...d6 is a failed attempt to challenge our pawns. 

Tactics flow from a better position, but they also flow from a position with more space and central control.

There isn't a good way to deal with BB5+.

rnbqkb1r/pppp1pp1/4pn1p/6B1/3PP3/8/PPP2P.text:
Now 3...h6, played roughly 20% of the time, is the subject of this study. 

Black wants us to either trade, or move the bishop away from the pin. Since moving away is bad (4.Bh4, Bf4, etc.) we'll trade.

The results of this trade are that the queen will go to f6, but Black loses an important minor piece that fought for central control.

rnbqkb1r/pppp1ppp/4pn2/6B1/3P4/8/PPP1PPP.text:
2...e6 is the most popular move.

We go for the Big Center.

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/5n2/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/R.text:
Black plays the flexible 1...Nf6.

But we take the game into our own theory with the Trompowsky.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
After seeing how to build a big center with the Trompowsky, there's another line we should consider. 

I'm talking about the direct 3...h6, where Black forces us to make a decision with our dark-squared bishop.

We'll open with the queen's pawn.

r1bq1rk1/ppp2pbp/3p1np1/5p2/2PP4/2N1P1P1.text:
And we will castle, having basically completed development.

This is the most common sequence of moves in the 2...g6 Trompowsky.

Here, one of the plans would be placing the queen on d3 and pushing the queenside pawns with a4 and b4 for a healthy expansion.

r1bq1rk1/pppn1pbp/3p2p1/5p2/2PP4/2N1P1P1.text:
Black develops as well.

They actually want to place the knight on f6, from where it will have a chance to control some central squares, and maybe even land on e4 to block our bishop.

We don't have to worry about that for now. We'll simply continue to develop.

r2q1rk1/pp2npbp/4bpp1/3p4/3P1N2/1QN1P1P1.text:
And a dagger in the position is definitely Qb3, attacking both the d5-pawn once again and the b7-pawn.

Our pressure is so great that we don't even have to rush capturing here.

We can just castle first.

r2q1rk1/pp2npbp/4bpp1/3p4/3P1N2/2N1P1P1/.text: Black is in time to defend, but look at their pieces.

r2q1rk1/pp3pbp/2n1bpp1/3p4/3P4/2N1P1P1/P.text:
Black has to maneuver to defend here, which will make their position extremely passive.

We'll attack the pawn with our three minor pieces.

rn1q1rk1/pp3pbp/4bpp1/3p4/3P4/2N1P1P1/PP.text:
Black defends d5 with the bishop, as there weren't any other real options.

But we won't stop adding attackers to the pawn. We play Nge2.

The knight is coming to f4.

rnbq1rk1/pp1p1pbp/2p2pp1/8/2PP4/2N1P3/PP.text:
Black could insist on playing ...d5, but that's actually good for us.

We'll look to fianchetto and await the expansion.

rnbq1rk1/pp3p1p/2pb1pp1/8/2BP4/2N1PN2/PP.text:
Which is fine, as we will make the space ourselves.

Having developed the knight to c3, we are in an equal but a very easy to play position.

On the queenside, a natural plan is Rb1 to support the b4-advance.

We should centralize the f-rook and play the prophylactic h3.

rnbq1rk1/pp3p1p/2pb1pp1/8/2BP4/4PN2/PP3P.text:
Black establishes some central presence here.

They don't want to give us too much space.

rnbq1rk1/pp3pbp/2p2pp1/3p4/2PP4/2N1P1P1/.text:
The point is to trade once it arrives.

And leave Black with an isolated pawn in the center.

rnbq1rk1/pp3pbp/5pp1/3p4/3P4/2N1P1P1/PP3.text:
Or an IQP, to be precise.

Now that pawn will be a clear target since it already can't advance and no pawn can defend it.

And we will start targeting it with the fianchetto.

rnbq1rk1/ppp2p1p/3b1pp1/8/2BP4/4PN2/PP3P.text:
Black castles...

And so will we.

There is no need to rush.

rnbq1rk1/ppp2pbp/3p1pp1/8/2PP4/2N1P3/PP3.text:
A much safer option than going for ...c6 and ...d5 is placing the pawn on d6.

Black gives up some central control but continues development.

We'll continue with our plan of fianchettoing.

Black won't be able to contest the long diagonal.

rnbq1rk1/ppp2pbp/3p2p1/5p2/2PP4/2N1P1P1/.text:
Expect to see this structure from Black in almost every setup here.

They have to play ...f5 to activate the bishop.

We'll just continue logically.

Our knight is coming to e2 next.

rnbq1rk1/pppp1pbp/5pp1/8/2PP4/4P3/PP3PPP.text:
In fact, after they castle...

We can activate the queenside knight first.

It's important to take as much control of d5 as possible.

rnbqk2r/ppp2p1p/3b1pp1/8/2BP4/4P3/PP3PPP.text:
Instead of going for the fianchetto, Black activates the bishop to d6 which is great for us, because they don't have a defender inbetween the pawns on the kingside.

Now that structure is just looking awkward.

We'll continue with simple development.

rnbqk2r/pppp1pbp/5pp1/8/3P4/4P3/PPP2PPP/.text:
Expect to see ...Bg7 here as much as 80% of the time, as it is the most logical move.

Black will most likely play ...f5 at some point to unleash the bishop, combined with either ...d6 or ...d5.

Since Black hasn't struck in the center yet, we will claim it.

We don't have to worry about not developing in time as Black has only got the bishop out.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2p1p/5pp1/3p4/3P4/4P3/PPP2PP.text:
Black going for ...d5 as early as move 4 is rare (only 7%), but does affect our setup.

Our bishop won't be as strong on g2 now since Black has a pawn on d5.

Instead, let's play c4 and challenge the center at once.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2p1p/5pp1/8/2pP4/4P3/PP3PPP/.text:
It's better for Black to capture than play ...c6 and leave themselves with an isolated pawn and a ruined pawn structure.

We will recapture with the bishop.

rnbqkb1r/pppp1p1p/5pp1/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/.text:
Black is forced to recapture with the e-pawn.

Now that we have exchanged our bishop, we will replace it with pawns on the dark squares to limit the opposing bishop. Thus we will play e3 here.

Our plan is simple: we want to fianchetto the light-squared bishop as that will be our power piece.

We'll castle and place the knights on e2 and c3, after we play c4 to expand in the center.

rnbqkb1r/pppppp1p/5np1/6B1/3P4/8/PPP1PPP.text:
Black aims for a fianchetto 15% of the time.

Against any d4 openings, going for the ...d6, ...g6 and ...Bg7 approach and playing in King's Indian style seems viable.

However, we won't let that happen so easily. Let's capture the knight.

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/5n2/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/R.text:
Black responds with ...Nf6.

And we'll play Bg5, the Trompowsky!

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
Let's see what happens if Black plays ...g6 on move 2 and goes for the early fianchetto in Chapter 2.

In fact, you will notice that we will get comfortable positions easy to play, following a specific developing pattern.

We will start with d4.

r1bqk2r/pp2bppp/2n1p3/6P1/3pN3/5N2/PPPQ1.text:
If they defend, we can pin this knight.

All of our pieces are active, with clear roles. 

We cannot say the same for Black.

r1bqk2r/ppp1ppbp/2n3p1/3p2P1/3P4/2N5/PPP.text:
Black attacks the d4-pawn.

We are now forced to defend the pawn, but playing e3 fits in with our overall plan.

r2qk2r/pp1bbppp/2n1p3/1B4P1/3NN3/8/PPPQ1.text:
Black is passive, and it's hard to suggest a move. 

Our increased space and piece activity is crushing. 

12...Nxd4 13.Qxd4 attacks both d7 and g7.

r2qk2r/pp1bbppp/2n1p3/1B4P1/3pN3/5N2/PPP.text: If they unpin, they block off the d-file and we can now take on d4.

r2qk2r/ppp1ppbp/2n3p1/3p1bP1/3P4/2N1P3/P.text: The bishop comes out to f5.

r2qk2r/ppp1ppbp/2n3p1/3p1bP1/3P4/2NBP3/P.text:
We don't mind trading light-squared bishops because we get rid of Black's bishop pair. 

A good plan is f4 and Nf3. 

Black will likely castle queenside in order to escape our h-file pressure.

r3k2r/pp1qppbp/2n3p1/3p2P1/3P4/2N2N2/PPP.text:
We simply defend. We have excellent h-file prospects. 

We want to tuck our king in with Kb1 and then see what Black does. 

One maneuver is Ne2, then c3, to make sure the d4-pawn is extra secure.

rn1qk2r/pbpp1ppp/1p2p3/6P1/1b1P4/2N2N2/P.text: If Black chooses to give up the bishop pair, we'll be happy.

rn1qk2r/pbpp1ppp/1p2p3/6P1/1b1P4/P1N2N2/.text:
We actually want to encourage them. 

8...Bxc3 9.Qxc3 and Black cannot win a pawn on g5 because 9...Bxf3 10.Qxf3 and we're attacking the rook on a8. 

We have more space and Black doesn't have a good pawn break without giving up the bishops.

rn1qk2r/pp1bppbp/6p1/1B1p2P1/3P4/2N5/PPP.text:
But we're okay with this block.

We are able to trade and now Black does not have a bishop pair advantage.

rn1qkb1r/pbpp1ppp/1p2p3/6P1/3P4/2N2N2/PP.text:
The bishop goes to b7.

Our plan will remain the same: Qd2 and 0-0-0. 

We also have to go Qd2 now to protect g5.

rn2k2r/pp1qppbp/6p1/3p2P1/3P4/2N5/PPPQ1P.text:
The queen recaptures.

We'll castle. The dust starts to settle. 

It is clear we have a strong asset in the g5-pawn.

rnbqk2r/pp1pppbp/6p1/2p3P1/3P4/2N5/PPPQP.text:
A smart idea from Black is to undermine our d4-pawn. 

If we make the mistake of taking on c5, we will give their bishop on g7 more squares.

That's why we'll simply defend the d4-pawn with e3 and try to stay solid on the dark squares.

rnbqk2r/pp1pppbp/6p1/6P1/3p4/2N1P3/PPPQ1.text:
Black wants trades to open up the position, because they have the bishop pair.

We'll simply recapture.

rnbqk2r/pp2bppp/4p3/2p3P1/3Pp3/2N2N2/PPP.text:
Black trades.

We'll recapture. The knight on e4 isn't easily removed. 

Our pawn on g5 now has an extra defender.

rnbqk2r/pp2bppp/4p3/2pp2P1/3P4/2N2N2/PPP.text:
They may try to undermine d4.

But we've got 8.e4 to open up the position! 

Since we are up in development, we don't mind if things become open.

rnbqk2r/pp2bppp/4p3/6P1/3pN3/5N2/PPPQ1PP.text:
Black takes on d4.

We can castle now.

Black does not have a way of holding on to the pawn.

rnbqk2r/pp2ppbp/6p1/3p2P1/3P4/2N5/PPPQ1P.text:
Black can resume in a normal way with 8...d5. 

This opens up their other bishop.

We can toss in a check with Bb5+ here. 

We know Black wouldn't want to play Nd7, so they'll likely block with 9...Nc6 (a self-pin), or 9...Bd7.

rnbqk2r/ppp1bppp/4p3/3p2P1/3P4/5N2/PPPQP.text:
6...d5 now is normal, establishing a pawn on the center.

We'll develop our other knight. We already have more space and better pieces. 

Black lost a lot of time developing their knight, jumping to e4 and then taking on g5.

rnbqk2r/ppp1ppbp/6p1/3p2P1/3P4/2N5/PPPQP.text:
Setups with 6...d5 are common. 

Black wants to gain some space in the center.

We'll castle. 

The rook on d1 also helps support d4 if the queen moves away.

rnbqk2r/ppppbppp/4p3/6P1/3P4/5N2/PPP1PPP.text:
Black aims at our g5-pawn.

This is the most popular variation and thus the main line of our study.

We will of course defend it, with the queen, also preparing 0-0-0.

rnbqk2r/ppppppbp/6p1/6P1/3P4/2N5/PPP1PPP.text:
Black fianchettoes. 

Their goal is to exert pressure on the dark squares. 

Our plan remains unaltered. 

We want to castle queenside, and put pawns on dark squares, neutralizing the fianchettoed bishop.

Our queen can move away to a useful square.

We have promising ideas of Bb5, or dxe5 to discover an attack on the g4-bishop.

A funny mistake could be 7...Bd6 8.dxe5 and both Black's bishops are under attack.

r3kb1r/pppq1p1p/2n2p2/3pp3/3P2b1/2P1PN2/.text:
The queen comes out to d7. 

Since the kingside is open, Black will likely go for ...0-0-0.

We should develop our other knight. 

Since our pawn is on c3, we go to d2.

rn1qk2r/pp3p1p/1b2bp2/3p3Q/4p3/1NN1P3/PP.text:
Black's huge issue is that they made themselves a weakness on d5. 

We will castle and win that pawn easily. We are winning.

rn1qkb1r/pp2pp1p/2p2p2/3p1b2/2PP4/4P3/PP.text:
Black defends d5.

We'll develop with Nc3, attacking the d5-pawn and increasing the pressure.

rn1qkb1r/pp3p1p/2p1pp2/3p1b2/2PP4/2N1P3/.text:
Here it's nice to see one of the main differences in the ...gxf6 variation. 

Black still has an e-pawn that they can defend d5 with.

rn1qkb1r/pp3p1p/2p1pp2/3p1b2/2PP4/2NBP3/.text:
If Black trades on d3, our queen is developed and we are happy. 

If they go to g6, we will simply continue with normal development like Nf3, and we could even push the h-pawn to attack the bishop. 

We can also insert the cxd5 capture so that our bishop isn't distracted with having to recapture on c4.

rn1qkb1r/ppp1pp1p/5p2/3p1b2/3P4/4P3/PPP2.text:
This occurs in 15% of games. 

The bishop comes out now so that e6 doesn't restrict it.

We'll undermine the center with c4.

rn1qkb1r/ppp2p1p/4pp2/3p1b2/2PP4/4P3/PP3.text:
Black defends d5 with 5...e6.

We should now take on d5.

rn1qkb1r/ppp2p1p/5p2/3pp3/3P2b1/4PN2/PPP.text:
Black could pin us, thinking that e4 will pose some practical problems. 

This is also a way of defending e5.

But we will calmly unpin with Be2.

rn2k2r/ppp2p1p/4pp2/3q1b2/1b1P4/2N1P3/PP.text:
But our idea is to recapture on c3 with our other knight and attack the queen once again. 

We have a plan of a3 and b4.

rn2kb1r/ppp2p1p/4pp2/3q1b2/3P4/4P3/PP3PP.text:
The queen recaptures, as 6...exd5 leaves Black with a horrible pawn structure.

But on d5 we can attack it and develop with tempo!

rnbqk2r/pp3p1p/1b3p2/3p4/4p3/1N2P3/PPP2P.text:
The bishop retreats to b6, where it keeps an eye on d4. 

This is a very normal-looking move, but it leads to good play for us.

We can develop and attack d5.

rnbqk2r/pp3p1p/5p2/2bp4/4p3/4P3/PPPN1PPP.text:
The bishop recaptures, but here it can be attacked.

Our knight also helps us control the outpost on d4. 

It seems this entire 6...c5 operation from Black is a total failure.

rnbqkb1r/pp3p1p/2p5/3p1p2/2PPp3/4P3/PP1N.text:
Black defends d5.

We are happy to capture on d5, fixing the weakness in place.

rnbqkb1r/pp3p1p/5p2/2pp4/3Pp3/4P3/PPPN1P.text:
Black may want to counter our center first.

Since we have a knight on d2, we can take the c-pawn and then move our knight with tempo on the bishop.

rnbqkb1r/pp3p1p/8/3p1p2/3Pp3/2N1P3/PP1N1.text:
We will have a lot of play against the d5-pawn. 

We want to play Be2 and develop, possibly castling queenside, but there is no immediate rush since we'd like to see what Black will do.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pp1p/5p2/3p4/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP.text:
Roughly 25% of the games in the database go like this. 

According to the engine, both recaptures are fine, so it's up to us to see what the main differences are. 

Black gets an open g-file, should they want to use it.

We will place our pawns on dark squares like always.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/3p2B1/3P4/8/PPP1PP.text:
Black focuses on gaining space in the center.

We'll take the knight to double the pawns.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2p1p/5p2/3p4/3Pp3/4PN2/PPP2P.text:
5...e4 isn't a challenge for us. 

Our knight is safe on d2 and it will help us pushing c4, undermining the pawns on the light squares.

The popular 6...Nc6 only blocks the c-pawn in and we can simply answer with 7.c4.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2p1p/5p2/3pp3/3P4/4P3/PPP2PP.text:
More than 30% of games continue like this. 

Black goes for this direct pawn break, which is a benefit of having recaptured 3...gxf6. They still have an e-pawn.

We should just develop our knight and attack the pawn.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2p1p/8/3p1p2/3Pp3/4P3/PPPN1P.text:
It's natural for Black to make use of this pawn.

They get a solid pawn chain.

But our plan of 7.c4 isn't stopped. We'll play it, and undermine the d5-pawn.

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/5n2/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/R.text:
Black develops their knight.

And we'll go for the Trompowsky.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
We will now see how play can be different if Black takes towards the center with the g-pawn when we exchange our bishop for the knight on f6.

Let's begin with 1.d4.

lessons.title: All Lines
lessons.chapter: The Hopton Attack (2.Bg5) vs The Dutch

r1b1kbr1/ppp1q3/2nppn2/5pp1/2BP4/2N1P1B1.text:
But our pieces are just better, and it's hard to suggest Black a way to make progress. 

White enjoys a stable edge.

r1b1kbr1/ppp1q3/2nppn2/5pp1/3P4/2N1P1B1/.text: Simple developing moves from Black can be played...

r1bqk2r/ppppp1bp/2n5/3N1pBp/3P4/4P3/PPP2.text: And White is better. Getting compensation was easy money.

rn1k1b1r/ppp2b2/5n1p/4pp1P/5Np1/4P1B1/PP.text: They lose castling rights when they recapture.

rn1k1b1r/ppp2b2/5nNp/4pp1P/6p1/4P1B1/PPP.text: And we unleash an attack on e5 and the rook.

rn1qkb1r/ppp1p3/3pbn1p/5p1P/3P2p1/4P1B1/.text:
The bishop is developed...

Our knight can come to f4,  defending h5.

rn1qkb1r/ppp1pb2/3p1n1p/5p1P/3P2p1/4P1B1.text:
So once the bishop goes to f7...

The knight arrives on f4, defending the pawn.

rn1qkb1r/ppp2b2/3p1n1p/4pp1P/3P1Np1/4P1B.text:
9...e5 doesn't work because...

We can just take.

rn1qkb1r/ppp2b2/5n1p/4pp1P/5Np1/4P1B1/PP.text:
Black recaptures.

We'll exchange queens and disrupt the black king's position.

rnb1kbnr/pp1pp1pp/1qp5/5pB1/3P4/4P3/PPP2.text:
If Black thinks they can just grab material and not give us activity, they have another think coming.

We can just ignore the threat and play Nd2.

rnb1kbnr/pp1pp1pp/2p5/5pB1/3P4/4P3/PqPN1.text:
It isn't a threat at all if the queen's position can be exploited.

We'll bring our rook to the semi-open b-file, attacking the black queen.

rnb1kbnr/pp1pp1pp/2p5/5pB1/3P4/q2BP3/P1P.text: Our vastly superior development is great compensation for the pawn.

rnb1kbnr/pp1pp1pp/2p5/5pB1/3P4/q3P3/P1PN.text: The queen gets out of the way.

rnb1kbr1/ppp1q3/3ppn2/5pp1/3P4/2N1P1B1/P.text: Now we can castle. If the position opens up, our pieces will come to life.

The queen is developed. Maybe e5 is an idea. 

Though because Black is so down in development, they shouldn't open up the position.

rnbq1rk1/pp4pp/2pbpn2/3p1pB1/2PP4/2NBPN2.text:
And so do we. 

We can come back to trade bishops on f4, bring our rook to the more active c-file, and in general enjoy a better position.

rnbqk1nr/pp2p1bp/2p3p1/3p1pB1/3P3P/2N1P3.text:
After adopting this light-square pawn structure...

We'll play Nf3, and Black must cope with various positional threats that we have in this position.

rnbqk1nr/ppp1p1bp/6p1/3p1pB1/3P3P/2N5/PP.text:
Black can react by putting a pawn in the center.

Now e3 prepares the development of our light-squared bishop.

rnbqk1nr/ppppp1b1/6pp/5pB1/3P3P/2N5/PPP1.text:
Attacking the bishop seems like a better try.

We'll just go back one square.

rnbqk1nr/ppppp1bp/6p1/5pB1/3P4/2N5/PPP1P.text:
The bishop goes to g7.

And here comes our h-pawn racing forward!

rnbqk2r/pp2p1bp/2p2np1/3p1pB1/3P3P/2N1PN.text: So if Black just continues with normal development...

rnbqk2r/pp2p1bp/2p2np1/3p1pB1/3P3P/2NBPN.text: We can have an advantage just by continuing to develop. Our pieces are more active, we have a lead in development and we have more space.

rnbqk2r/pp4pp/2p2p2/3p1p2/1bPP4/2N1P3/PP.text:
Black can get into a lot of trouble quickly...

We can attack the bishop and add more pressure on d5.

rnbqk2r/pp4pp/2p2p2/3p1p2/2PP4/1QP1P3/P4.text:
Whose center is more impressive? 

At this point the engine is even recommending giving up material with 8...f4 because of how superior our structure is! Of course, we would just take that!

rnbqk2r/pp4pp/2pbpn2/3p1pB1/2PP4/2N1PN2/.text:
And just with simple development, because of space and structure, White is better.

We'll develop our last minor piece.

rnbqk2r/ppppp1b1/5npp/5p2/3P1B1P/2NQ4/PP.text:
And now in a very unorthodox way, we can develop the queen. 

Black needs to be careful against our threat of Qg3, double attacking c7 and g6.

Additionally, we have e4 ideas and 0-0-0.

rnbqk2r/ppppp1bp/5np1/5pB1/3P3P/2N5/PPP1.text:
4...Nf6 allows us to destroy the kingside:

We push forward! The pawn structure will be changed one way or the other.

rnbqk2r/ppppp1bp/6p1/5pBn/3P4/2N5/PPP1PP.text:
If the knight takes...

We'll have enough compensation for this exchange.

rnbqk2r/ppppp1bp/8/5pBp/3P4/2N5/PPP1PPP1.text:
Black recaptures and the pawns are wrecked.

We can attack e7 with Nd5.

rnbqkb1r/pp4pp/2p1pn2/3p1pB1/2PP4/2N1P3/.text:
It's possible for Black to go for this setup.

In which case we should just develop our pieces...

rnbqkb1r/pp4pp/2p2p2/3p1p2/2PP4/4P3/PP3P.text:
5...c6 is lousy. Even taking in the middle is good, because either Black will have an IQP in a bad structure or they'll lose central control.

But quite honestly we could just continue building up pressure against that pawn with Nc3.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1p1pp/5n2/3p1pB1/3P4/4P3/PPP.text:
The black knight is developed.

Let's attack d5!

rnbqkb1r/ppp1p3/3p1n1p/5p2/3P2pP/4P1B1/P.text:
If 6...g4...

h5 prevents Black from playing h5 themselves, supporting g4, and it gives the h4 square back to the bishop.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1p3/3p1n1p/5pp1/3P4/4P1B1/PP.text:
Black sets up counterplay with future pawn breaks.

But we'll play h4 and achieve a pawn break of our own!

rnbqkb1r/ppp3pp/4pn2/3p1pB1/2PP4/4P3/PP3.text:
Black defends.

We'll develop and put pressure on d5 once more.

rnbqkb1r/ppp3pp/5p2/3p1p2/3P4/4P3/PPP2PP.text:
Black goes d5, controlling the center.

But we'll immediately challenge Black's control by playing c4.

rnbqkb1r/pppp2pp/5p2/5p2/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/.text:
exf6 is the only move that doesn't lose.

We'll begin putting our pawns on dark squares.

rnbqkb1r/ppppp1pp/5n2/5pB1/3P4/8/PPP1PPP.text:
2...Nf6 is the most popular, but not the best. 

The reason for that is because we can damage the pawns.

We'll just take. It seems the move 1...f5 here isn't beneficial for Black.

rnbqkb1r/ppppp2p/5p2/5p2/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/.text: If this move is played, notice the weakness on h5...

rnbqkb1r/ppppp2p/5p2/5p2/3PP3/8/PPP2PPP/.text: Black will lose castling rights. White has a winning position.

rnbqkb1r/ppppp3/5n1p/5pp1/3P4/6B1/PPP1PP.text:
Nf6 covers the h5 square.

But now we can just cover the f4 square.

rnbqkbnr/pp1pp1pp/2p5/5pB1/3P4/8/PPP1PPP.text:
Black may have ideas of pawn hunting.

We can just develop normally.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1p1pp/8/3p1pB1/3P4/8/PPP1PPP.text:
2...d5 is also popular.

Now e3 is a good developing move.

rnbqkbnr/ppppp1p1/7p/5pB1/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP.text:
2...h6 is very popular at the amateur level: the bishop is such a nuisance that Black wants to remove it immediately.

I suggest we just stay on the diagonal that perturbs Black the most.

rnbqkbnr/ppppp1pp/8/5p2/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/R.text:
And then our opponents go for the Dutch right away.

We can still play Bg5 here! This is the Hopton Attack. 

The bishop can prove disruptive to Black.

rnbqkbnr/ppppp2p/6p1/5pB1/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP.text:
The move most masters play is 2...g6.

Let's just develop aggressively with Nc3!

rnbqkbnr/ppppp3/7p/5pp1/3P3B/8/PPP1PPPP/.text:
Tactically speaking, our bishop won't get trapped.

I suggest we retreat to g3.

rnbqkbnr/ppppp3/7p/6p1/3P1p2/4P1B1/PPP2P.text: e3 attacks the f4 pawn and opens up the threat of checkmate on h5.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
I want to make sure you are not surprised when facing the Dutch Defense (1...f5). 

You will learn how to take Dutch Defense players out of their comfort zone! Let's begin with 1.d4.

rnbqkbr1/ppp1p3/3p1n1p/5pp1/3P3P/4P1B1/P.text:
Moving the rook off the h-file is another option.

In which case I suggest trading on g5...

rnbqkbr1/ppp1p3/3p1n2/5pp1/3P4/4P1B1/PPP.text:
Black recaptures.

We won't be castling kingside, since our rook is happy on the h-file. So let's develop the queenside pieces.
